newsitem.title: JAPAN: In Japan, a woman's place is still not in politics.
newsitem.headline: In Japan, a woman's place is still not in politics.

text.p: Japanese women are no longer confined solely to the domestic sphere, but neither are they finding much of a home in national politics -- as the forthcoming general election shows.
A record number of women are standing as candidates in Sunday's vote, but they are only around 10 percent of the total. Most are affiliated with marginal parties.

"Women's voting rate is actually higher than that of men, but their political consciousness is lower. They need...real access to political power," said Keiko Kihira, president of the League of Women Voters in Tokyo.
And despite the fact that women make up more than half Japan's 98 million voters, virtually no candidates are making efforts to woo them directly by promoting women's issues.

"Although the parties are playing very much to issues that concern women, such as the consumption tax, it seems to me that women and women's issues, directly, are just not a part of this campaign," said John Neuffer, a senior research fellow at Mitsui Marine Research Institute.
Japanese women first gained the right to vote in 1945 with the passage of women's suffrage legislation that year. In the 1947 general election 85 stood as candidates.
That figure was not exceeded until this election, with a record 153 women standing out of 1,503 candidates altogether.

Activists say the small number is mainly due to the political establishment's reluctance to back strong female candidates, as well as a reluctance among women to enter what is still seen as male territory.
Japanese tradition dictated that a woman's place was in the home so strongly that words meaning wife translate as "a person inside the house" or "Mrs Interior" -- a feeling that lingers.
"Men choose the candidates, and they don't really want to put up politically active, ordinary women. They want women who will win easily, women who are well known," Kihira said.
"In this situation, unless a woman is very strong and has a lot of courage, she won't put herself forward."

But Hatoko Shimizu, president of the Housewives' League, disagreed. Citing growing numbers of women in city or regional politics, she said the problem is not one of willingness to enter the political fray, but economics.

"At the national level, everything to do with politics takes a tremendous amount of money, even putting up posters. Political contributors feel it's much more to their benefit to put money into male candidates," she added.

A majority of the women candidates are affiliated with various opposition parties, with the largest number -- 66, or nearly half the total -- sponsored by the Japan Communist Party. The newborn Democratic Party is second with 22, while Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) is backing 16.
The Social Democratic Party is headed by one of the few high-profile women in Japanese politics, Takako Doi.
By contrast, the old-guard Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), forecast by polls to take a majority, is backing a mere 10 women among 355 candidates altogether.
"Women's status is a really weak point of LDP policy," said Haruo Arima, election chief at the Japan Communist Party.
"Women's position is an important barometer of how developed a society is, and we want to work actively to have more women in politics," he added.

Some women have always played an essential role in Japanese politics, including wives working for spouses too busy in Tokyo to spend time in their districts. Even Kumiko Hashimoto, wife of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, does not escape this duty.

But the picture for woman candidates remains dark. Both Kihira and Shimizu lamented the fact that major parties tend to favour female candidates whose major grace is a well-known face. This year a baseball team manager's wife is being sponsored by Shinshinto.
"Political parties remain a man's world, and they still like decorative women better. Those women always get money," Shimizu said.
